blocks.text: Antibiotics are drugs that treat bacterial infections by killing bacteria or stopping their growth. They are classified mainly by their mechanism of action and chemical structure. The four major classes are penicillins, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones and sulfonamides.

blocks.alt: A bacterial cell with a thick green cell wall, a looped DNA molecule with an orange enzyme on it, purple ribosomes and a red box labelled folate. Labels: penicillin acts on the cell wall, tetracycline on the 30S ribosome subunit, fluoroquinolones on DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, and sulfonamides on folate synthesis.
blocks.caption: Where the four antibiotic classes act on a bacterial cell (original diagram after Figure 23.1).
blocks.long_description: Antibiotics act on structures or processes that bacteria have and human cells lack or have in a different form. Penicillin stops the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall, so the wall fails and the cell bursts (bactericidal). Tetracycline binds the 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes and stops aminoacyl-tRNA reaching the A site, halting protein synthesis (bacteriostatic). Fluoroquinolones trap DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, causing double-strand DNA breaks (bactericidal). Sulfonamides block the making of folate, needed for DNA synthesis (bacteriostatic). Human cells have no cell wall, have 80S ribosomes and take folate from food, so they are spared.

blocks.title: Bactericidal and bacteriostatic
blocks.text: A bactericidal drug kills bacteria; a bacteriostatic drug stops them growing and multiplying, leaving the immune system to destroy them.
